extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, and practitioners litigating or studying judicial remedies for agency rulemaking and adjudication
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrinal criteria for when courts should vacate, remand, or excuse agency rulemaking or orders for procedural (notice-and-comment) or explanatory failures, and when a context-sensitive harmlessness/prejudice inquiry is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material alteration of obligations requires notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment that materially alters the obligations of regulated firms (i.e., expands the scope of stringent requirements to more regulated objects) cannot be adopted without notice-and-comment because affected parties are "greatly interested" and deserve the opportunity to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EPA's change measuring PCB contamination by surface concentration (an obvious mistake) materially altered obligations for porous surfaces and, despite the agency's characterization as a technical correction, the D.C. Circuit held the change required notice-and-comment and vacated the rule. Courts look to whether the change meaningfully affects regulated parties' obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception cannot rest on bald assertions that comments would be unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may invoke the APA's good-cause exception (when notice and comment are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest), but courts will not accept mere assertions that further comment is 'unnecessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation: 'Bald assertions that the agency does not believe comments would be useful cannot create good cause to forgo notice and comment procedures.' Example: CAB's attempt to avoid a second comment period by claiming the existing record made further comments unnecessary was rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice/harmlessness factors for excusing notice-and-comment violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should consider whether the challenging party has suffered actual prejudice from the agency's procedural error by asking whether (a) the party had a full and fair opportunity to voice objections, (b) the agency heard and considered the substantive concerns the party would have raised, or (c) there is no substantial reason to think that the party's comments would have led the agency to change its mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context-sensitive inquiry: close working relationships and prior engagement between agencies and regulated parties (e.g., meetings, internet bulletins of anticipated corrections, invited contributions) can support a finding of no prejudice. If challengers 'raised and fiercely debated' the same arguments previously, that demonstrates presence of actual notice and absence of new arguments on remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict harmlessness standard (many lower courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonly applied standard treats notice-and-comment failures as presumptively prejudicial: the failure is harmless only where the agency's mistake 'clearly had no bearing on the procedure used or the substance of decision reached.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: Read literally, this test makes it nearly impossible to show lack of prejudice because skipping notice and comment necessarily bears on procedure; it forces agencies into an untenable position of arguing they would have 'clearly' not changed their minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitive 'invigorated' rule of prejudicial error (proposed/analogous statutory standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts could adopt a more discriminating prejudice inquiry analogous to the Clean Air Act's instruction: invalidate for procedural errors 'only if the errors were so serious and related to matters of such central relevance to the rule that there is a substantial likelihood that the rule would have been significantly changed if such errors had not been made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is tailor-made to require remedial restraint in a subset of cases and would permit courts to uphold agency actions when procedural errors were not central to the substance of the rule. The APA does not prevent courts from adopting this gloss on §706's 'rule of prejudicial error.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of record in prejudice inquiry: generally limited but potentially broader
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts generally confine their inquiry to the record generated during notice-and-comment, the APA instructs reviewing courts to review 'the whole record,' and outside formal proceedings that record can include whatever influenced the agency's decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: Courts limit extra-record inquiry to avoid allowing agencies to base decisions on undisclosed materials that would undermine the purpose of notice-and-comment. Once a procedural deficiency is identified, courts deciding remedy should consider whether examining broader materials is appropriate to determine actual prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery rule: courts review only the grounds the agency actually relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing court may not uphold an agency action on alternative grounds the agency offered only in litigation rather than those the agency itself relied on at the time of decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Upholding on litigation-posted justifications would intrude into the agency's domain and undermine incentives for agencies to make determinations and provide reasons at the time they act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic benefits of vacatur under Chenery (incentive function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vacating defective agency decisions serves systemic functions: (1) it encourages agencies to proceed by rulemaking rather than ad hoc adjudication, and (2) it forces agencies to offer nonarbitrary reasons at the time of decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when vacatur seems wasteful in individual cases, these systemic incentives justify vacatur in some circumstances; but the article argues Chenery need not be absolute to preserve these benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendly's limiting principle to Chenery (when reversal is unwarranted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vacatur is unnecessary when an agency errs with respect to subsidiary factual findings but adequate alternative facts support the agency's decision and there is no reason to believe the agency would reconsider if apprised of its mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Friendly recommended that courts be receptive to reasons implicit in the determination and avoid causing needless expense and delay by vacating where the underlying decision would stand on remand; courts have been reluctant to embrace this limit fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophylactic rules may be relaxed where exclusion costs outweigh benefits (Miranda analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophylactic judicial rules (like Chenery) need not be enforced absolutely in all contexts; if the systemic benefits of strict application are slight and the costs of remediation large, courts may confine prophylactic rules to contexts where their concerns are implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Miranda's prophylactic exclusions have recognized exceptions (e.g., routine traffic stops, public-safety questions); similarly, administrative-law prophylaxis might be relaxed in discrete categories where benefits of vacatur are minimal compared to costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prill requirement: agencies must exercise interpretive discretion when statutes are ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Prill and related caselaw, when a statute is ambiguous, an agency must recognize the ambiguity and explain why it chose one permissible interpretation over another; failure to do so can constitute a Chenery-type violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prill cases differ from ordinary Chenery mistakes: agencies often take pragmatic statutory readings, agency actions (including enforcement) can demonstrate a preference for an interpretation, agencies can usually reinstate their prior decision on remand, and courts may be identifying only marginal ambiguities—punishing agencies for not ventilating unlikely alternatives can be excessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three distinguishing features of Prill cases that counsel against automatic vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing Prill-type failures, courts should account for (1) agencies' pragmatic statutory-construction practices (the agency's chosen reading is probative of its preference), (2) the agency's actions often show it prefers the adopted interpretation (so remand is unlikely to change the outcome), and (3) determining statutory ambiguity can be difficult and marginal ambiguities should not trigger punitive vacatur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: DEA's PDK and Postal Regulatory Commission cases illustrate that vacatur and remand sometimes produce only a 'ping-pong' of decisions and little substantive change; courts should be cautious about requiring boilerplate rejection of marginal alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of distinct remedial approaches for orders versus rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have quietly developed two remedial approaches—one primarily for orders and another for rules—to soften the blunt application of Chenery, although these doctrinal innovations are tenuous and contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These approaches reflect judicial recognition that costs of remedial purity can be large; they attempt to allow remedial discretion (e.g., upholding where no prejudice or where reinstatement on remand is likely) but have not been fully embraced by higher courts.
